title: Fall and head injury in an older woman

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Mrs Castellan, I'm Dr Pemberton. And you are?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'm her daughter, Sue.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thanks for coming in with her. Mrs Castellan, can you tell me what happened?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I tripped on the rug in the hall and banged my head on the door frame.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What time was that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About half past nine.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Mum, it was before that. The post hadn't come and you hadn't had your breakfast. It was about quarter to eight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Was it? Oh, she's probably right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: So about quarter to eight. Which side did you hit?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This side. The left, by my eye.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you black out at all?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I wasn't there when she fell, but when I got there about ten minutes later she was a bit muddled. She kept asking what day it was. That lasted maybe ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you remember that, Mrs Castellan?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I don't remember Sue arriving.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you been sick at all?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She was sick once in the car on the way here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Was I? I don't remember that either.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any headache now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit of a headache where I hit it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any problems with your vision, or weakness in your arms or legs?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any neck pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, my neck's fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you trip, or did you feel dizzy or faint before you fell?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I caught my foot on the rug. I wasn't dizzy.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What medicines are you on?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I've got the list. Apixaban, 2.5 milligrams twice a day, for her heart rhythm. Bisoprolol 2.5 milligrams once a day. And amlodipine 5.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: So you're on a blood thinner. When did you last take the apixaban?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This morning, with my breakfast. After I fell.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Penicillin. It makes me swell up.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. Let me examine you. Your eyes are open, you're talking to me normally and you can follow instructions, so your Glasgow Coma Score is 15. There's a cut here, about 3 centimetres long, on your left temple, with a bump around it. Your pupils are equal and react to light. Squeeze my hands, push your feet down. Strength is normal everywhere.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm pressing on the back of your neck. Any pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your heart rate is irregular at about 80, and your blood pressure is 146 over 82.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: What happens now?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Because your mum is on a blood thinner, she needs a CT scan of her head, to make sure there's no bleeding inside. We'll do that within the next few hours.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm going to hold off this evening's dose of apixaban until we've seen the scan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: All right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: The nurse will clean the cut and close it with steri-strips. Are you up to date with your tetanus?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I had all of them.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If the scan is normal, you can go home with Sue. Someone needs to stay with you for the next 24 hours.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll stay with her.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Great. If she becomes drowsy, confused, vomits again, has a worsening headache, a fit, or any weakness, call 999 or bring her straight back.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay, I will.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Head injury after a mechanical fall at home at about 07:45.
reference_note.history: Tripped on a rug and struck the left side of her head on a door frame. Daughter reports she seemed muddled for about 10 minutes afterwards; patient has no memory of this. Loss of consciousness uncertain (unwitnessed). One episode of vomiting in the car. Mild headache at the impact site. No visual disturbance, limb weakness or neck pain. No preceding dizziness or presyncope. Last apixaban dose this morning, after the fall. Tetanus up to date.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (atrial fibrillation). Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily. Amlodipine 5 mg once daily. Allergic to penicillin (swelling).
reference_note.examination: GCS 15. 3 cm laceration with haematoma over the left temple. Pupils equal and reactive. Normal power in all limbs. No cervical spine midline tenderness. HR 80 irregular, BP 146/82.
reference_note.impression: Head injury in an anticoagulated 81-year-old with brief post-traumatic confusion and amnesia, and one episode of vomiting.
reference_note.plan: CT head (anticoagulated). Withhold this evening's apixaban dose until CT head reviewed. Wound cleaned and closed with steri-strips. If CT normal, discharge with daughter, who will stay with her for 24 hours.
reference_note.safety_netting: Call 999 or return immediately if drowsy, confused, further vomiting, worsening headache, seizure or limb weakness. Written head injury advice given to daughter.

mutations.seeded_rationale: Anticoagulation is a key reason for an urgent CT head; if it is missing from the record, a reviewer may deprioritise the scan or restart dosing, although her symptoms after the head injury make it likely she would still be scanned.
mutations.description: Blood thinner dropped from a head injury note

mutations.seeded_rationale: The wound is visible, so the wrong side is likely to be noticed, but it could confuse CT correlation and wound review.
mutations.description: Laceration recorded on the wrong side

mutations.seeded_rationale: The daughter corrected the time; the injury time affects CT timing decisions and the observation period.
mutations.description: Fall time kept at the figure the daughter corrected

mutations.seeded_rationale: Amlodipine recorded as amiloride, a look-alike/sound-alike pair; if she is admitted, medicines reconciliation from this note would give an 81-year-old a potassium-sparing diuretic instead of her antihypertensive, risking hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.

mutations.original_text: One episode of vomiting in the car.
mutations.seeded_rationale: Vomiting after a head injury is a risk factor for intracranial injury; recording it as absent may lower the urgency of CT and observation.
mutations.description: Vomiting after head injury recorded as absent

mutations.original_text: Daughter reports she seemed muddled for about 10 minutes afterwards; patient has no memory of this.
mutations.mutated_text: Patient reports feeling muddled for about 10 minutes afterwards.
mutations.seeded_rationale: Attributing the report to the patient hides that she has amnesia for the episode, which is itself a marker of significant head injury.
mutations.description: Daughter's account recorded as the patient's

mutations.original_text: Withhold this evening's apixaban dose until CT head reviewed.
mutations.seeded_rationale: Continuing anticoagulation before an intracranial bleed is excluded could worsen any haemorrhage.
mutations.description: Apixaban hold dropped from the plan

mutations.seeded_rationale: Penicillin recorded as penicillamine, a recognised sound-alike pair; the true allergy (swelling, suggesting angioedema) is lost, so a penicillin could be given if she develops an infection in hospital.
